questions.a: 'The boy was praised (by the teacher).' boy→subject, praised→was praised (be carries past). A wrong answer 'the boy is praised' reveals the student changed the verb form but let the tense drift — the be-auxiliary must carry the original tense.

'My watch has been stolen.' Note the agent 'someone' is vague → deleted, not 'by someone'. A wrong answer 'my watch has stolen' shows the student forgot the be+V3 compound — participle alone can't carry voice.

questions.q: Should this go passive? 'My grandmother knitted this sweater for me.' Defend.
questions.a: Debatable, but staying active is defensible — the doer (grandmother) carries the emotional point. 'This sweater was knitted for me by my grandmother' buries the person who matters. A wrong answer mechanically passivizing reveals the student treats voice as a trick, not a meaning choice — the examiners' exact complaint.

questions.q: Passive voice moves the object to subject ______ and demotes or deletes the doer: object→subject, verb→be+V3, subject→(by + agent, often dropped).

Fill in the blank: Show the surgery on one sentence: 'The cat chased the mouse.' Object 'the mouse' walks to the front; 'chased' becomes 'was chased' (be + V3, be ______ the tense); 'the cat' demotes to 'by the cat' or vanishes.
Fill in the blank: Passive voice moves the object to subject position and demotes or deletes the doer: object→subject, verb→be+V______, subject→(by + agent, often dropped).
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student converts all tenses active↔passive, preserves tense through the be-auxiliary, handles the double-object verbs (give/tell/teach) both ways, and knows when the agent must stay ('The storm destroyed…' vs anomalous cases).
